hook: A 4-bit float can only hold sixteen values. Blackwell GPUs train and serve frontier models with it anyway. Here is how.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — A 4-bit float can only hold sixteen values. Blackwell GPUs train and serve frontier models with it anyway. Here is how.
0:15 QUESTION — DeepSeek-V3 trained in FP8. gpt-oss shipped its MoE weights in MXFP4. If you cannot draw the bits of these formats, you cannot reason about why one works and another overflows.
1:00 INTUITION — A float is a ruler with log spacing. Exponent bits buy range, mantissa bits buy resolution. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — value = (-1)^s * 2^(e - bias) * (1 + m / 2^M) for normals; subnormals drop the implicit 1. bf16 keeps fp32's 8 exponent bits, so same range, 7 mantissa bits. fp16 has 5 exponent bits, max 65504. FP8 E4M3 max is 448, no infinity. E5M2 max is 57344, keeps inf and NaN. FP4 E2M1 has exactly these magnitudes: 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6. That is why it needs block scales: MXFP4 shares one E8M0 power-of-two scale per 32 elements, NVFP4 uses an FP8 E4M3 scale per 16 elements plus one FP32 per-tensor scale.

6:00 CODE — Write decode_float(bits, E, M, bias) that returns the value for any layout. Enumerate all 256 FP8 codes for E4M3 and E5M2, all 16 E2M1 codes. Plot representable values on a log axis. Then fp4_block_quant(x, block=32, scale='e8m0') and block=16 with an e4m3 scale.

9:00 RECEIPT — assert max of my E4M3 table equals torch.finfo(torch.float8_e4m3fn).max, which is 448. Same for float8_e5m2 at 57344. Round-trip a random tensor through torch.float8_e4m3fn and through my decoder; torch.equal on the values.
10:30 MEASURE — Mean squared error of MXFP4 vs NVFP4 on a real Qwen3 weight matrix. NVFP4 should win because smaller blocks and a finer scale.
12:00 TAKEAWAY — Exponent bits are range, mantissa bits are precision, and at 4 bits the block scale does most of the work. Interview line: FP4 only works because each tiny block gets its own scale.
12:30 NEXT — Next: Absmax and zero-point quantization
key_math: x = (-1)^s * 2^(e-bias) * (1 + m/2^M); E4M3 max = 448, E5M2 max = 57344; E2M1 magnitudes {0,0.5,1,1.5,2,3,4,6}; MXFP4: x_i ~ 2^k * e2m1_i over 32 elements, NVFP4: x_i ~ s_tensor * s_block(e4m3) * e2m1_i over 16 elements
code_task: decode_float(bits:int, E:int, M:int, bias:int) -> float; table_fp8(fmt) -> Tensor[256]; table_e2m1() -> Tensor[16]; fp4_block_quant(x:[N], block:int, scale_fmt:str) -> (codes:[N] uint8, scales:[N/block]); plot of representable values on log axis.
receipt: assert table_fp8('e4m3').abs().max() == torch.finfo(torch.float8_e4m3fn).max == 448; assert table_fp8('e5m2').abs().max() == 57344; torch.equal(my_decode(x.to(torch.float8_e4m3fn).view(torch.uint8)), x.to(torch.float8_e4m3fn).float()).
gotchas: E4M3fn has no infinity and uses the all-ones mantissa at max exponent for NaN, so naive IEEE logic gives the wrong max; forgetting subnormals makes tiny values snap to zero; casting to float8 in PyTorch saturates or produces NaN depending on version, so clamp to +-448 yourself.
interview_q: Why does DeepSeek-V3 use E4M3 for all tensors instead of E5M2 for gradients? Model answer: fine-grained per-tile scaling handles range, so the extra mantissa bit of E4M3 buys more accuracy than E5M2's extra range.
explainer: We start with thirty-two bits of an fp32 number, colored by role: one sign bit, eight exponent bits, twenty-three mantissa bits.
Now we shrink the mantissa to seven bits and keep the exponent. That is bf16, same range as fp32, much coarser steps.
Here fp16 trades the other way. Five exponent bits, ten mantissa bits, and the largest number it can hold is 65504.
Next the two FP8 formats side by side. E4M3 stops at 448, E5M2 reaches 57344 but with half the resolution.
Every representable value goes on a log number line as a tick. Notice the ticks are evenly spaced within each power of two.
At four bits we have only sixteen ticks: zero, one half, one, one and a half, two, three, four, six.
So we give each block its own scale. MXFP4 shares a power of two across thirty-two values, NVFP4 an FP8 scale across sixteen.
The error heatmap shows smaller blocks with finer scales track the real weights much better. That is the whole trick.

bit boxes animate shrinking to 16 bits, label bf16, range bar unchanged
fp16 layout with range bar ending at 65504
two FP8 layouts stacked with range bars 448 and 57344
log-scale number line with tick marks per format, zoom on one octave
16 dots on a line labeled with E2M1 values
weight vector split into blocks of 32 and 16, each with a scale badge
two heatmaps of quantization error, MXFP4 vs NVFP4
short: The E2M1 sixteen-value number line beat. Caption: 'This is every number FP4 can store.'
yt_title: FP8, FP4, MXFP4 and NVFP4 explained: every bit, plotted
x_post: FP4 (E2M1) can store exactly 16 values: 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6 and negatives. MXFP4 and NVFP4 work because each block of 32 or 16 gets its own scale. I enumerated every code and plotted them. Code + video:
linkedin: Today I wrote a decoder for every low-precision float format: bf16, fp16, FP8 E4M3/E5M2 and FP4 E2M1. My tables match torch.finfo exactly (448 and 57344). On a real Qwen3 weight matrix, NVFP4's 16-element blocks beat MXFP4's 32-element blocks on error. The block scale is doing most of the work at 4 bits.

hook: Quantization is two lines of code. One outlier in your tensor quietly turns most of those 256 int8 levels into zeros.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Quantization is two lines of code. One outlier in your tensor quietly turns most of those 256 int8 levels into zeros.

0:15 QUESTION — Every int8 and int4 model on Hugging Face, from Llama to Qwen, starts from one of two mappings. Symmetric absmax, or asymmetric with a zero-point. Pick wrong and you waste half your bits.
1:00 INTUITION — Quantizing is laying a ruler with 2^b ticks over your data. Absmax centers the ruler at zero. Zero-point slides it to cover exactly min to max. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Absmax int8: s = 127 / max|x|, q = round(s * x), x_hat = q / s. Zero-point b bits: s = (2^b - 1) / (max - min), z = -round(min * s), q = clamp(round(s * x) + z, 0, 2^b - 1), x_hat = (q - z) / s. Rounding error is at most 1/(2s) per element, so error scales with the range, which is why one outlier hurts everyone. After ReLU or softmax the data is one-sided, so absmax wastes the negative half.

6:00 CODE — absmax_quant(x, bits) -> (q int8, scale); absmax_dequant(q, scale). zp_quant(x, bits) -> (q uint8, scale, zero); zp_dequant. Error metrics: mse, max_abs_err, SQNR in dB = 10 log10(sum x^2 / sum (x - x_hat)^2). Test on Gaussian, on post-ReLU data, and on Gaussian plus one value of 100.

9:00 RECEIPT — Compare to PyTorch: torch.quantize_per_tensor(x, scale=1/s, zero_point=z, dtype=torch.quint8).int_repr() equals my q exactly, and .dequantize() matches my x_hat with assert_close. Note PyTorch's scale is the step size, the inverse of mine.
10:30 MEASURE — SQNR table: symmetric vs asymmetric on three distributions, at 8 and 4 bits. Then sweep the outlier from 1 to 1000 and plot SQNR collapsing.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — Error is proportional to range, so the whole field is about shrinking the range each scale has to cover. Interview line: absmax for zero-centered weights, zero-point for one-sided activations.
12:30 NEXT — Next: Granularity: per-tensor, per-channel, per-group
key_math: s = 127 / max|x|, q = round(s x); s = (2^b - 1)/(max - min), z = -round(min * s), q = clamp(round(s x) + z, 0, 2^b - 1), x_hat = (q - z)/s; SQNR = 10 log10(||x||^2 / ||x - x_hat||^2)
code_task: absmax_quant(x:Tensor[N], bits:int) -> (q:int8[N], s:float); zp_quant(x, bits) -> (q:uint8[N], s, z:int); dequant functions; sqnr(x, x_hat) -> dB; outlier sweep plot.
receipt: torch.equal(my_q, torch.quantize_per_tensor(x, 1/s, z, torch.quint8).int_repr()); torch.testing.assert_close(my_xhat, qt.dequantize()); expect SQNR about 40 dB for int8 absmax on N(0,1) data.
gotchas: PyTorch's scale is the step size (1/s in my notation), so passing s directly gives garbage; torch.round uses round-half-to-even, so a hand rolled floor(x+0.5) differs on exact .5 values; zero-point outside [0, 2^b - 1] when data does not include zero, so clamp z or include 0 in the range.
interview_q: When would you use asymmetric over symmetric quantization? Model answer: for one-sided distributions like post-ReLU or post-softmax activations, a zero-point uses all 2^b levels; for roughly symmetric weights, absmax is simpler and avoids the zero-point term in the matmul.
explainer: We plot a histogram of real values and lay a ruler with two hundred fifty-six ticks over it.
Absmax puts zero in the middle and stretches the ruler to the largest absolute value. Every tick is one step of size one over s.
Each value snaps to its nearest tick. The gap between value and tick is the rounding error, never more than half a step.
Now the data is all positive, like after a ReLU. Half of the absmax ruler covers nothing at all.
The zero-point ruler slides to start at the minimum. All two hundred fifty-six ticks land where the data lives.
We add one outlier at one hundred. The ruler stretches to reach it, and the ticks spread apart.
Most values now fall into the same few ticks near zero. The signal to noise curve drops off a cliff.
The lesson on screen: error is proportional to range. Next we will shrink the range with more scales.

symmetric ruler centered at 0, scale label
dots snapping to ticks with small error arrows
one-sided histogram, empty left half of ruler shaded red
ruler sliding right, z label appears

short: The outlier beat. Caption: 'One number ruined my int8 tensor.'
yt_title: Absmax vs Zero-Point Quantization from Scratch (matches PyTorch)
x_post: Int8 quantization error is proportional to range. Add one value of 100 to a Gaussian tensor and SQNR collapses, because most values land in a handful of ticks near zero. Built absmax and zero-point from scratch, bit-exact vs torch.quantize_per_tensor. Code + video:
linkedin: Today I implemented absmax and zero-point quantization from scratch and matched torch.quantize_per_tensor bit for bit. On N(0,1) data int8 absmax gives about 40 dB SQNR; one outlier at 100 drops it sharply. Everything after this in quantization is a way to shrink the range each scale covers.

hook: Why is the number 128 hiding in GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF and torchao? Because it is where the error curve flattens.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Why is the number 128 hiding in GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF and torchao? Because it is where the error curve flattens.

0:15 QUESTION — Last episode, error scales with range. So give more values their own scale. But every scale costs bits. Llama and Qwen int4 checkpoints almost all use group size 128. We will measure why.
1:00 INTUITION — One ruler for the whole tensor, one per output row, or one per 128 weights. More rulers fit the data tighter but you have to store them. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Weight W is [out, in]. Per-tensor: one s. Per-channel: s_i = 127 / max_j |W_ij|, shape [out, 1]. Per-group: reshape to [out, in/g, g], s shape [out, in/g, 1]. Storage overhead in bits per weight = scale_bits / g, so fp16 scales at g=128 cost 0.125 bits, making int4 effectively 4.125 bits (4.25 with a zero-point). Per-channel on weights is free at matmul time because the scale factors out of the dot product along in; per-group is not, which is why it needs a dequant inside the kernel.

5:30 CODE — quantize_groupwise(W, bits, group_size) -> (q, scales, zeros) using W.reshape(out, in // g, g). group_size=-1 means per-channel, group_size=W.numel() means per-tensor. Load Qwen3-0.6B, loop over every nn.Linear, compute relative Frobenius error ||W - W_hat|| / ||W|| for g in {per-tensor, per-channel, 1024, 256, 128, 64, 32} at 4 and 8 bits.

9:00 RECEIPT — Quantize one layer with torchao's int4 weight-only config at group_size=128 (quantize_(model, Int4WeightOnlyConfig(group_size=128))), dequantize its weight, and check my group-128 error is within a few percent of torchao's on the same layer. Exact bits can differ because torchao uses its own zero-point and rounding convention.
10:30 MEASURE — Table and plot: error vs group size, with effective bits per weight on the second axis. The knee should sit between 64 and 128.
12:00 TAKEAWAY — Group size 128 is the knee: most of the error reduction for an eighth of a bit. Interview line: per-group trades a little storage for fitting each scale to a local range.
12:30 NEXT — Next: LLM.int8() and outlier features
key_math: per-group: W.reshape(out, in/g, g), s = (2^(b-1) - 1)/max|W_group|; overhead = scale_bits/g bits per weight; rel_err = ||W - W_hat||_F / ||W||_F
code_task: quantize_groupwise(W:[out,in], bits:int, group_size:int) -> (q:[out,in] int, scales:[out,in/g], zeros:[out,in/g]); dequantize_groupwise(...) -> [out,in]; sweep over all nn.Linear in Qwen3-0.6B producing an error vs group-size table.
receipt: For one Qwen3-0.6B q_proj, my group-128 int4 relative error vs torchao Int4WeightOnlyConfig(group_size=128) dequantized weight relative error: agree within about 5%; per-tensor int4 error should be several times larger than group-128.
gotchas: in_features not divisible by g crashes the reshape, so pad or assert; grouping along the wrong axis (out instead of in) breaks the kernel layout every library expects; torchao int4 kernels need bf16 and a CUDA GPU, so on Mac compare dequantized weights only.
interview_q: Why is per-channel weight quantization free in a matmul but per-group is not? Model answer: a per-output-channel scale multiplies the whole dot product so it can be applied after accumulation; per-group scales change along the reduction dimension, so the kernel must dequantize inside the inner loop.
explainer: We show a weight matrix as a heatmap. One scale for the whole thing means the hottest pixel sets the step for everyone.
Now each row gets its own scale. Rows with small weights finally get fine steps of their own.
Next we cut every row into groups of one hundred twenty-eight. Each group gets a little scale badge beside it.
The error heatmap cools down group by group as the scales tighten around local ranges.
But every badge costs sixteen bits. We draw a bar for storage overhead growing as groups shrink.
Plot the two curves together: error falling, bits rising. The knee sits right around one hundred twenty-eight.
That is why GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF and torchao all default near this number. It is a measured tradeoff, not folklore.

per-row scale column appears to the right

short: The dual-axis knee plot. Caption: 'Why every int4 model uses group size 128.'
yt_title: Per-Group Quantization: why group size 128 is everywhere
x_post: Group size 128 shows up in GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF and torchao. Measured on Qwen3-0.6B: error drops fast until about 128, then flattens, while fp16 scales cost 16/g bits per weight. At g=128, int4 is really 4.125 bits. Code + video:
linkedin: Today I measured int4 quantization error across per-tensor, per-channel and per-group scales on every linear layer of Qwen3-0.6B. The curve has a clear knee near group size 128, for just 0.125 extra bits per weight. Now I know why every int4 checkpoint uses it.

hook: Around 6.7 billion parameters, a few hidden dimensions start carrying values 20 times bigger than the rest. Naive int8 dies right there.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Around 6.7 billion parameters, a few hidden dimensions start carrying values 20 times bigger than the rest. Naive int8 dies right there.

0:15 QUESTION — Dettmers found that per-tensor int8 inference works for small OPT models then falls apart near 6.7B. The cause is a handful of outlier feature dimensions. bitsandbytes load_in_8bit exists because of this.

1:00 INTUITION — Imagine a classroom where one student shouts. Everyone else whispers. If you set the volume knob for the shouter, you cannot hear anyone else. So you give the shouter a separate microphone. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Vector-wise quantization: X [T, d] gets a scale per row c_x, W [d, out] a scale per column c_w. XW ~ (1 / (c_x outer c_w)) * (X_i8 @ W_i8). Mixed-precision decomposition: O = {j : max_t |X_tj| >= 6.0}. XW = X[:, O] @ W[O, :] in fp16 + dequant(X_i8[:, not O] @ W_i8[not O, :]). Outliers are about 0.1% of dims but removing them breaks perplexity, which is why you keep them in fp16 instead of clipping.

6:00 CODE — Register forward hooks on every nn.Linear input of Qwen3-8B or Llama-2-7B in bf16. For each layer record per-dim max |x| over 128 calibration sequences. Find dims above 6.0, count them per layer, and check whether the same dim indices repeat across layers. Then write int8_vectorwise_matmul(X, W) and llm_int8_matmul(X, W, threshold=6.0).

9:00 RECEIPT — Compare to bitsandbytes: load the same model with BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_8bit=True, llm_int8_threshold=6.0) and check wikitext-2 perplexity of my llm_int8 layer swap is within 0.05 of bnb. Also ablation: zero out the outlier dims and watch perplexity explode.
10:30 MEASURE — Heatmap of max |x| per layer per dim with outlier columns lighting up. Perplexity: bf16, naive per-tensor int8, vector-wise int8, LLM.int8 with decomposition.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — Outliers are few, systematic and essential, so you route around them rather than clip them. Interview line: LLM.int8 keeps outlier feature dims in fp16 and runs the other 99.9% in int8.
12:30 NEXT — Next: Weight-only vs W8A8, and SmoothQuant
key_math: XW ~ (X_i8 W_i8) / (c_x c_w^T); O = {j : max_t |X_tj| >= 6}; XW = X_O W_O (fp16) + dequant(X_{~O} W_{~O}) (int8)
code_task: collect_act_stats(model, loader) -> {layer: Tensor[d] max_abs}; find_outliers(stats, thr=6.0) -> {layer: idx}; int8_vectorwise_matmul(X:[T,d], W:[d,out]) -> [T,out]; llm_int8_matmul(X, W, threshold=6.0) -> [T,out]; layer swap and wikitext-2 perplexity.
receipt: abs(ppl_mine - ppl_bnb_load_in_8bit) < 0.05 on wikitext-2 for the same model and context length; naive per-tensor int8 perplexity noticeably worse; zeroing outlier dims blows perplexity up by a large factor.
gotchas: Hooks on bf16 activations need .float() before max or you lose precision; outlier stats depend on calibration text, so use real text not random tokens; bitsandbytes 8-bit is often slower than bf16 on modern GPUs, it saves memory not time.
interview_q: Why can't you just clip activation outliers to make int8 work? Model answer: the outlier dimensions carry important information; Dettmers showed zeroing them destroys perplexity, so they must be kept in higher precision or migrated into weights like SmoothQuant does.
explainer: We open a real Llama layer and plot the largest activation in every hidden dimension as a bar.
Most bars are short. A few dimensions tower over the rest, around twenty times taller.
We stack every layer as a heatmap. The same columns light up layer after layer. These are systematic outliers.
A single per-tensor scale is set by the tallest bar, so every normal value rounds to almost nothing.
Vector-wise quantization gives each row of X and each column of W its own scale. Better, but outliers still stretch their rows.
So we split the matmul. Outlier columns go through an fp16 path, the other ninety-nine point nine percent through int8.
The two results add back together, and perplexity lands right on top of the bf16 baseline.

yt_title: LLM.int8() Outlier Features: finding them in a real 7B model
x_post: Hooked every linear input of a 7B model: a handful of hidden dims carry values 20x larger than the rest, the same dims in every layer. Per-tensor int8 dies; LLM.int8 routes them through fp16 and matches bf16 perplexity. Code + video:
linkedin: Today I found the outlier features from the LLM.int8() paper in a real 7B model by hooking every linear input. A few dimensions dominate, and they repeat across layers. My mixed-precision int8 matmul matched bitsandbytes perplexity within 0.05, and zeroing those dims wrecked the model.

hook: You cannot quantize activations with outliers. So SmoothQuant moves the outliers into the weights, where quantization does not mind.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — You cannot quantize activations with outliers. So SmoothQuant moves the outliers into the weights, where quantization does not mind.

0:15 QUESTION — W4A16 shrinks memory and speeds up decode. W8A8 uses int8 tensor cores and speeds up prefill and big batches. But W8A8 needs quantized activations, and last episode showed activations have outliers.

1:00 INTUITION — Two kids on a seesaw. Activations are the heavy one, weights are light. A per-channel scale lets you slide weight from one side to the other without changing the product. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Y = X W = (X diag(s)^-1)(diag(s) W), exact for any s > 0. Choose s_j = max|X_j|^α / max|W_j|^(1-α). With α = 0.5, both sides end up with max sqrt(max|X_j| max|W_j|) in channel j, so neither has outliers. diag(s)^-1 folds into the previous LayerNorm or RMSNorm weight offline, diag(s) folds into W, so there is zero runtime cost. Compute bound vs memory bound: weight-only helps decode at batch 1, W8A8 helps prefill where matmuls are compute bound.

6:00 CODE — Calibrate per-channel max|X_j| on 128 samples. smooth_scales(x_max, W, alpha) -> s [d]. apply_smoothing(norm, linears, s): norm.weight /= s, each linear.weight *= s along in. Then fake-quant W8A8: per-token int8 for X, per-channel int8 for W. Run on Qwen3-8B or Llama-2-7B, alpha in {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1}.

9:30 RECEIPT — assert_close(model_smoothed(x), model(x)) before quantization, proving the transform is exact up to bf16 rounding. Then wikitext-2 perplexity: naive W8A8 vs SmoothQuant W8A8 vs bf16. The paper reports SmoothQuant W8A8 matching FP16 on OPT-175B where naive W8A8 collapses; expect a smaller but clear gap on 7B.
11:00 MEASURE — Per-channel max histograms of X and W before and after smoothing. Perplexity vs alpha curve.

12:30 TAKEAWAY — SmoothQuant is a free, exact rescaling that moves quantization difficulty from activations to weights. Interview line: pick weight-only for memory-bound decode, W8A8 with smoothing for compute-bound serving.
13:00 NEXT — Next: GPTQ, derived
key_math: Y = (X diag(s)^-1)(diag(s) W); s_j = max|X_j|^α / max|W_j|^(1-α), α = 0.5; per-token act scale c_t = 127/max_j|X_tj|, per-channel weight scale
code_task: calibrate_act_max(model, loader) -> {layer: Tensor[d]}; smooth_scales(x_max:[d], W:[out,d], alpha) -> s:[d]; apply_smoothing(norm, [q,k,v] or [gate,up], s); fake_quant_w8a8(linear) wrapper; perplexity sweep over alpha.
receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(smoothed_model(ids).logits, base_model(ids).logits, atol=2e-2, rtol=2e-2) in bf16 before quantization; then ppl(SmoothQuant W8A8) much closer to bf16 than ppl(naive W8A8) on wikitext-2.
gotchas: You can only fold diag(s)^-1 into a preceding norm when every consumer of that norm output gets the same s, so q, k and v must share one s; o_proj and down_proj have no preceding norm to fold into, so they need a different treatment or stay unsmoothed; alpha too high pushes outliers into weights and breaks weight quantization instead.
interview_q: When does weight-only int4 beat W8A8, and vice versa? Model answer: at small batch decode the matmuls are memory bound, so fewer weight bytes wins; at large batch or prefill they are compute bound, so int8 tensor cores with quantized activations win.
explainer: We put activation channel maxima on the left and weight channel maxima on the right, as bar charts.
The activation bars have spikes. The weight bars are flat and calm. Quantizing activations is the hard side.
We draw a seesaw between them. Dividing activations by s and multiplying weights by s leaves the product unchanged.
With alpha equal one half, each channel's scale is a geometric mean, and both sides meet in the middle.
After smoothing, the activation spikes are gone and the weight bars are only a little bumpier.
The division by s disappears into the previous RMSNorm weight, so the model runs exactly as before.
Now both sides quantize cleanly to int8, and the perplexity bar returns close to the bf16 line.

short: The seesaw beat. Caption: 'Move the outliers where they do not hurt.'
yt_title: SmoothQuant from Scratch: W8A8 without the outlier pain
x_post: SmoothQuant in one line: Y = (X diag(s)^-1)(diag(s) W), with s_j = max|X_j|^0.5 / max|W_j|^0.5. Exact, folds into the RMSNorm, zero runtime cost, and it makes W8A8 work. Verified the transform is exact before quantizing. Code + video:
linkedin: Today I built SmoothQuant from scratch on a 7B model. The per-channel rescale is mathematically exact, folds into the previous RMSNorm, and moves activation outliers into the weights. Naive W8A8 hurt perplexity; smoothed W8A8 came back near bf16. I also learned when weight-only beats W8A8: it depends on whether you are memory or compute bound.

hook: Round-to-nearest treats every weight alone. GPTQ quantizes one column, then nudges every remaining column to cancel the error it just made.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Round-to-nearest treats every weight alone. GPTQ quantizes one column, then nudges every remaining column to cancel the error it just made.

0:15 QUESTION — GPTQ made 4-bit LLMs practical in 2022 and still powers a large share of int4 checkpoints. It quantizes a 175B model in hours with no retraining. The idea comes from a 1993 pruning paper.

1:00 INTUITION — You round a column of weights and the layer output drifts. But the other weights are still free. Adjust them to pull the output back. The Hessian tells you which direction to pull. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Objective per layer: minimize ||W X - W_hat X||^2 over quantized W_hat, rows independent. Hessian of that is H = 2 X X^T, shape [in, in]. Optimal Brain Surgeon: removing or fixing weight q with error e forces the best update of the others: delta = -(e / [H^-1]_qq) * H^-1[:, q]. GPTQ processes columns in fixed order for all rows at once: err = (W[:, q] - quant(W[:, q])) / Hinv[q, q]; W[:, q+1:] -= err outer Hinv[q, q+1:]. Then remove q from H^-1. The trick: those successive inverses are rows of the upper Cholesky factor of H^-1, so you compute it once. Dampen with H += 0.01 * mean(diag H) * I for stability. Lazy batching: update a block of 128 columns, then apply the accumulated error to the rest in one matmul.

7:30 CODE — Hook one Linear in Llama-2-7B or Qwen3-8B, accumulate H = 2/N * sum x x^T over 128 calibration sequences of 2048 tokens. gptq_quantize(W [out,in], H [in,in], bits=4, group_size=128, blocksize=128): damp, Hinv = cholesky_inverse(cholesky(H)), then cholesky(Hinv, upper=True); loop columns, quantize with group scales computed when entering each group, propagate error.

10:30 RECEIPT — Layer reconstruction error ||W X - W_hat X||^2 / ||W X||^2: GPTQ must be clearly below RTN at the same group size. End to end on Llama-2-7B W4 g128, the AWQ paper reports wikitext-2 perplexity FP16 5.47, RTN 5.73, GPTQ 5.69; reproduce within about 0.05 using my GPTQ on every layer sequentially.
12:00 MEASURE — Bar chart: relative output error for RTN vs GPTQ at 4 and 3 bits on one layer. At 3 bits the gap is much larger.

13:00 TAKEAWAY — GPTQ is OBS applied column by column with one Cholesky factor. Interview line: it uses second-order calibration statistics to let unquantized weights absorb each column's rounding error.
13:30 NEXT — Next: AWQ
key_math: H = 2 X X^T; H <- H + 0.01 mean(diag H) I; err_q = (w_q - quant(w_q)) / [H^-1]_qq; W[:, q+1:] -= err_q [H^-1]_{q, q+1:} (using upper Cholesky of H^-1)
code_task: accumulate_hessian(layer, loader) -> H:[in,in] fp32; gptq_quantize(W:[out,in], H:[in,in], bits=4, group_size=128, blocksize=128) -> (W_hat:[out,in], scales:[out,in/128], zeros); rtn_quantize for baseline; sequential layer-by-layer driver feeding quantized outputs forward.
receipt: rel_err_gptq < rel_err_rtn on the same layer and group size; full Llama-2-7B W4 g128 wikitext-2 ppl within ~0.05 of the 5.69 the AWQ paper reports for GPTQ, and below my RTN number (paper: 5.73).
gotchas: Accumulating H in bf16 overflows or loses precision, keep it fp32; dead input channels make H singular, so set H[i,i]=1 and W[:,i]=0 where diag is zero plus damping; computing group scales up front instead of when the column loop enters a group ignores the updates GPTQ already made.
interview_q: Why does GPTQ need calibration data but RTN does not? Model answer: GPTQ minimizes output error ||WX - W_hat X|| rather than weight error, so it needs the input covariance X X^T to know which directions matter and how to redistribute rounding error.
explainer: We show a weight matrix and a column cursor at the left edge. GPTQ will walk across it one column at a time.
The first column snaps to the int4 grid. A red error vector appears where it moved.
Instead of ignoring that error, we spread it into every column to the right, weighted by the inverse Hessian row.
The Hessian is just two X X transpose. It encodes which input directions the layer really uses.
After each step, that column is frozen. The cursor moves on and the remaining columns have already absorbed the error.
Computing a new inverse each step would be slow. One Cholesky factor gives us every row we need, in order.
We batch updates in blocks of one hundred twenty-eight columns, so most work becomes one big matmul.
Final scoreboard on screen: output error for round to nearest versus GPTQ, at four bits and at three bits.

x_post: GPTQ in two lines: err = (w_q - quant(w_q)) / Hinv[q,q]; W[:, q+1:] -= err * Hinv[q, q+1:], with H = 2XX^T and one upper Cholesky of H^-1. Beat RTN on every layer of a 7B model at 4 bits. Code + video:
linkedin: Today I derived GPTQ from Optimal Brain Surgeon and implemented it from scratch. Each quantized column's error gets redistributed to the remaining columns via the inverse Hessian, computed once with a Cholesky factor. On Llama-2-7B at 4 bits, group 128, I compared my perplexity against the 5.69 reported in the AWQ paper's table. This is the core of my low-precision project.

hook: One percent of weight channels matter far more than the rest. AWQ finds them from activations and protects them with a scale, no fp16 needed.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — One percent of weight channels matter far more than the rest. AWQ finds them from activations and protects them with a scale, no fp16 needed.
0:15 QUESTION — AWQ won best paper at MLSys 2024 and is the default int4 format in many serving stacks. It needs no backprop and no Hessian, just a grid search over one number per layer.

1:00 INTUITION — Weights that multiply big activations cause big output error when rounded. Scale those weights up before rounding and their relative error shrinks. Undo the scale on the activation side. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Keeping just ~1% salient channels in fp16 recovers most of the RTN loss, but mixed precision is hardware unfriendly. Instead: Q(w * s) * (x / s). Rounding error per weight is about half a step, and the step barely changes when you scale a few channels, so the relative error on salient channels shrinks by about 1/s. Choose s = s_X^α, where s_X is the per-input-channel mean |x|. Search α in [0, 1] on a 20-point grid to minimize ||Q(W diag(s)) (diag(s)^-1 X) - W X||. Like SmoothQuant, diag(s)^-1 folds into the previous op, but here the goal is weight error, not activation range.

6:30 CODE — Calibrate mean |x| per input channel. awq_search(W [out,in], X [N,in], bits=4, group_size=128, n_grid=20) -> best_s: for each alpha, s = x_mean.pow(alpha).clamp(min=1e-4), normalize s by sqrt(max * min), W_q = rtn_groupwise(W * s) / s, loss = mse(X @ W_q.T, X @ W.T). Also an fp16-salient baseline: keep top 1% channels by activation magnitude unquantized.

9:30 RECEIPT — Layer output error: AWQ < RTN, and close to the keep-1%-in-fp16 baseline. Compare my chosen scales against the AutoAWQ or llm-compressor scales for the same layer (direction and magnitude, not bit exact). End to end Llama-2-7B W4 g128 wikitext-2: the AWQ paper reports 5.60 vs RTN 5.73 vs GPTQ 5.69.
11:00 MEASURE — Loss vs alpha curve for three layers (qkv, o_proj, down_proj). Note where the optimum lands; down_proj usually wants a larger alpha.

12:30 TAKEAWAY — AWQ protects salient weights by scaling, choosing the scale from activations with a one-dimensional search. Interview line: GPTQ compensates error after rounding; AWQ reshapes weights so rounding hurts less.
13:00 NEXT — Next: Quantize a model: perplexity vs speed
key_math: s = s_X^α, α* = argmin_{α in [0,1]} ||Q(W diag(s)) (diag(s)^-1 X) - W X||^2; s_X,j = mean_t |X_tj|
code_task: act_mean_abs(layer, loader) -> [in]; awq_search(W:[out,in], X:[N,in], bits, group_size, n_grid=20) -> (alpha*, s:[in]); apply_awq_scale(prev_op, linears, s); rtn_groupwise; keep_salient_fp16 baseline.
receipt: mse_awq < mse_rtn for every searched layer and within ~20% of the keep-top-1%-fp16 baseline; full model W4 g128 wikitext-2 ppl compared to the AWQ paper's reported 5.60 (RTN 5.73, FP16 5.47).
gotchas: Searching alpha with the wrong activation statistic (max instead of mean) gives a worse optimum; without normalizing s, the overall scale shifts group ranges and the search becomes noisy; q, k, v share an input so they must share one s, just like SmoothQuant.
interview_q: How does AWQ differ from GPTQ? Model answer: AWQ picks per-channel scales from activation magnitudes so salient weights get finer effective resolution, with no weight updates; GPTQ quantizes column by column and updates the remaining weights using second-order information. They can be combined.
explainer: We show input activations as a bar chart. A few channels average much larger magnitudes than the others.
The matching weight columns are highlighted in gold. Rounding these particular weights moves the output the most.
Keeping them in fp16 fixes most of the error, but mixed precision kernels are awkward, so we want another way.
We multiply those salient columns by a scale s before rounding. The grid step stays almost the same.
Relative error on those weights shrinks by about one over s, and we divide the activation by s to compensate.
The scale comes from the activation mean raised to a power alpha. We sweep twenty values of alpha.
The loss curve dips to a minimum. That alpha becomes the layer's scale, folded into the previous op for free.

short: The scale-then-round beat. Caption: 'Protect 1% of weights without fp16.'
x_post: AWQ: scale salient weight channels by s = mean|x|^alpha before rounding, divide activations by s after. Search 20 alphas per layer, no backprop, no Hessian. Beat RTN on every layer and landed close to keeping the top 1% in fp16. Code + video:
linkedin: Today I implemented AWQ's scale search from scratch. Activation magnitudes identify the ~1% of weight channels that matter most, and a single exponent alpha per layer protects them through scaling instead of mixed precision. My layer errors beat round-to-nearest everywhere. GPTQ and AWQ are now both in my low-precision toolkit.

hook: Int4 makes a model four times smaller. It does not make it four times faster. Here are the real numbers on one RTX 4090.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Int4 makes a model four times smaller. It does not make it four times faster. Here are the real numbers on one RTX 4090.

0:15 QUESTION — You have built absmax, groups, LLM.int8, SmoothQuant, GPTQ and AWQ. Now the practitioner question: which library, which bits, and what do you actually get in memory, perplexity and tokens per second on Qwen3-8B or Llama-2-7B?
1:00 INTUITION — Decode at batch 1 is reading every weight once per token. Fewer bytes means faster, until dequantization overhead and kernel quality eat the gain. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Upper bound on decode tokens/s = memory bandwidth / bytes of weights. 4090 is about 1 TB/s. 8B params: bf16 16 GB gives about 60 tok/s ceiling, int8 about 120, int4 at 4.125 bits about 4.1 GB gives about 240. Real numbers fall short because of KV cache reads, dequant math and launch overhead. Perplexity = exp(mean NLL) on wikitext-2 at fixed context.

4:00 CODE — One harness, five configs: bf16 baseline; bitsandbytes 8-bit and 4-bit NF4 via BitsAndBytesConfig; torchao quantize_(model, Int8WeightOnlyConfig()) and quantize_(model, Int4WeightOnlyConfig(group_size=128)) with torch.compile; my GPTQ and AWQ checkpoints; GGUF Q4_K_M via llama.cpp (convert and quantize with its tools, see llama.cpp docs for exact script names). Measure peak memory with torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated, decode tok/s at batch 1 over 256 tokens after warmup, wikitext-2 perplexity at 2048 context.

9:00 RECEIPT — bf16 perplexity must match the published baseline for the model (Llama-2-7B wikitext-2 5.47 at 2048 context per the AWQ paper) within 0.02, which proves the harness is right. Memory ratios must be close to bits ratios. Each int4 perplexity should sit within a few percent of bf16.
10:30 MEASURE — The table: method, bits, memory GB, perplexity, decode tok/s, percent of bandwidth ceiling. Then a scatter of perplexity vs tok/s.

12:30 TAKEAWAY — Memory scales with bits; speed scales with kernel quality. Interview line: quantization is a bandwidth play for decode, so measure percent of the memory-bandwidth roofline, not just tok/s. This table is the baseline for project P8, where I write my own W4A16 Triton kernel.
13:00 NEXT — Next: KV cache quantization and FP8 inference
key_math: tok/s_max ~ BW / weight_bytes; weight_bytes = N_params * bits/8 (+ scale overhead bits/g); ppl = exp((1/T) sum -log p(x_t | x_<t))
code_task: bench(model, tokenizer) -> dict(mem_gb, ppl, tok_s); configs list for bf16, bnb int8, bnb nf4, torchao int8/int4 weight-only, own GPTQ/AWQ, llama.cpp Q4_K_M; results table and scatter plot.
receipt: bf16 wikitext-2 ppl for Llama-2-7B at 2048 context within 0.02 of 5.47; int4 g128 memory about 0.27x of bf16; every int4 config ppl within ~5% of bf16; report decode tok/s as percent of 1 TB/s / weight_bytes.
gotchas: Benchmarking without warmup and torch.cuda.synchronize gives fantasy numbers; perplexity depends on context length and stride, so fix both across configs; torchao int4 is only fast with torch.compile and bf16 on CUDA, bitsandbytes 4-bit can be slower than bf16 at batch 1.
interview_q: Why doesn't 4-bit quantization give 4x faster inference? Model answer: decode is memory bound, so the ceiling improves roughly with bytes, but KV cache reads, dequantization compute, non-quantized layers and kernel launch overhead all eat into it; at large batch the workload turns compute bound and weight-only quantization helps less.
explainer: We draw one GPU memory bar per configuration. bf16 Qwen fills sixteen gigabytes. Int4 fits in about four.
Next to each bar we draw the decode speed ceiling: memory bandwidth divided by weight bytes.
Then the measured speed drops in as a solid bar. Every method falls short of its ceiling by a different amount.
The gap is dequantization math, KV cache reads and kernel quality. A good int4 kernel closes most of it.
Now perplexity. All the four bit methods cluster just above the bf16 line, with AWQ and GPTQ lowest.
The scatter plot puts perplexity against tokens per second. The best methods sit in the bottom right corner.

x_post: Benchmarked bf16, bnb int8/NF4, torchao int4, my GPTQ and AWQ, and GGUF Q4_K_M on one RTX 4090. Memory tracks bits almost perfectly. Speed tracks kernel quality. Report percent of the bandwidth ceiling, not just tok/s. Code + video:
linkedin: Today I built one benchmark harness and ran every quantization method I know on a 7B-class model on an RTX 4090: memory, wikitext-2 perplexity and decode tokens per second. Memory scaled with bits; speed did not, because kernels and dequant overhead matter. This table is the baseline for my next project: a W4A16 Triton kernel.

hook: At long context the KV cache outweighs the model. Storing it in FP8 doubles how many users fit on the same GPU.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — At long context the KV cache outweighs the model. Storing it in FP8 doubles how many users fit on the same GPU.

0:15 QUESTION — Serving engines like vLLM and SGLang run out of KV cache before they run out of compute. Quantizing weights does nothing for that. So engines offer an FP8 KV cache. What does it cost in quality?
1:00 INTUITION — Every token you have seen leaves behind a key and a value per layer. Halve their bytes and you double the tokens that fit. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — KV bytes per token = 2 * L * n_kv * d_head * bytes. Qwen3-8B: 36 layers, 8 KV heads, d_head 128, so 2*36*8*128*2 = 147,456 bytes, about 144 KiB per token in bf16, 72 KiB in FP8. At 32k tokens that is about 4.5 GB vs 2.25 GB per sequence. Per-tensor FP8 E4M3 with scale s = 448 / max|K|; per-head or per-token scales cut error further. Keys have outlier channels (RoPE dims), values are better behaved, so keys usually need finer scales.

5:30 CODE — Extend the KV cache from M13 style generation: kv_quant(k, fmt) -> (k_q, scale) storing torch.float8_e4m3fn or int8 with per-head scales; dequantize inside attention before F.scaled_dot_product_attention. Variants: bf16, fp8 per-tensor, fp8 per-head, int8 per-token. Measure cache bytes, max batch at 8k context in 24 GB, and wikitext-2 perplexity at 4k context.

9:00 RECEIPT — My KV bytes per token equal the formula exactly for Qwen3-8B (147,456 in bf16). Then launch vLLM with --kv-cache-dtype fp8 and compare the KV cache capacity it reports in its startup log, which should roughly double vs the default, and check my fp8 perplexity delta is in the same range as vLLM's output quality on a fixed eval.
10:30 MEASURE — Table: format, bytes/token, max concurrent 8k sequences on a 4090, perplexity delta. Plot of per-channel key magnitude showing the outlier channels.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — KV cache quantization buys concurrency, not single-request speed, and keys are harder than values. Interview line: for long-context serving, FP8 KV is often the single biggest capacity win. This feeds directly into featherserve, project P2.
12:30 NEXT — Next: Quantization-aware training and FP8 training
key_math: KV_bytes/token = 2 * L * n_kv * d_head * bytes; Qwen3-8B: 2*36*8*128*2 = 147,456 B; s_fp8 = 448 / max|K| (per tensor or per head); max_batch = free_mem / (KV_bytes/token * seq_len)
code_task: kv_bytes_per_token(cfg, dtype) -> int; QuantKVCache with append(k:[B,n_kv,T,d], v) storing fp8/int8 + scales and get() dequantizing to bf16; attention via F.scaled_dot_product_attention; perplexity and capacity sweep.
receipt: assert kv_bytes_per_token(qwen3_8b_cfg, torch.bfloat16) == 147456; vLLM launched with --kv-cache-dtype fp8 reports roughly 2x the KV cache token capacity of the default in its startup log; fp8 per-head perplexity within ~1% of bf16.
gotchas: Forgetting GQA and using n_heads instead of n_kv_heads overestimates the cache by the group factor; casting to float8 without clamping to +-448 yields NaN; quantizing keys before RoPE vs after changes error, so be consistent with what the engine does.
interview_q: How much KV cache does a 32k context request use on an 8B GQA model, and how do you cut it? Model answer: 2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes per token, about 144 KiB for Qwen3-8B in bf16, so about 4.5 GB at 32k; FP8 KV halves it, and GQA, MLA or sliding windows cut it architecturally.
explainer: We draw one token's KV cache as a stack: thirty-six layers, each with eight key heads and eight value heads.
Each head is a strip of one hundred twenty-eight numbers in bf16. Multiply it out, about one hundred forty-four kilobytes per token.
Now stretch to thirty-two thousand tokens. The cache bar grows past the size of a quantized model.
We cast every strip to FP8. Each number shrinks from two bytes to one, and the bar halves.
Keys show a few bright outlier channels from RoPE. Per-head scales keep them from crushing the rest.
Back on the GPU memory chart, twice as many user sequences now fit in the same twenty-four gigabytes.

short: The cache-outgrows-the-model beat. Caption: 'At 32k context, the KV cache is the model.'
yt_title: KV Cache Quantization: FP8 KV doubles your serving capacity
x_post: Qwen3-8B KV cache: 2*36*8*128*2 = 147,456 bytes per token in bf16, about 4.5 GB at 32k context. FP8 halves it with a small perplexity cost, and keys are harder than values. Built it, then checked against vLLM --kv-cache-dtype fp8. Code + video:
linkedin: Today I quantized the KV cache, not the weights. For Qwen3-8B the cache is 144 KiB per token in bf16, so at long context it rivals the model. FP8 with per-head scales halved it with a small perplexity cost, and vLLM's FP8 KV option confirmed the capacity doubling. This goes straight into my inference engine project.

hook: Post-training quantization rounds a model it never warned. Quantization-aware training lets the model practice being rounded, and FP8 training skips the rounding entirely.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Post-training quantization rounds a model it never warned. Quantization-aware training lets the model practice being rounded, and FP8 training skips the rounding entirely.

0:15 QUESTION — Meta and Google ship QAT versions of their small models because int4 PTQ loses too much at small scale. DeepSeek-V3 trained in FP8 end to end. Both rest on one trick: a gradient through round().

1:00 INTUITION — round() is a staircase. Its gradient is zero almost everywhere. So during backward we pretend it is a straight line. That lie is the straight-through estimator. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Fake quant: x_hat = s^-1 * clamp(round(s x), -q_max, q_max). Forward uses x_hat. Backward STE: d x_hat / d x = 1 inside the clamp range, 0 outside. In PyTorch: x_hat = x + (fake_quant(x) - x).detach(). FP8 training is different: real FP8 matmuls with per-tensor or per-block scales, master weights kept in higher precision. Delayed scaling uses the amax history of past steps; current scaling computes amax now. DeepSeek-V3 uses 1x128 tiles for activations and 128x128 blocks for weights.

5:00 CODE — fake_quant_ste(x, bits, group_size) using the detach trick. QATLinear(nn.Linear) that fake-quantizes its weight int4 g128 in forward. Train a small GPT from M06 on TinyStories to convergence in bf16, then three arms: PTQ int4 RTN, QAT int4 for the last 10% of steps, and FP8 training with torchao's float8 conversion (convert_to_float8_training) on a GPU that supports FP8. Note the 4090 supports FP8 tensor cores.

9:00 RECEIPT — Gradient check: torch.autograd.grad of fake_quant_ste(x).sum() equals 1 inside range and 0 outside. QAT model after real int4 conversion: val loss closer to bf16 than PTQ. torchao FP8 training loss curve overlaps the bf16 curve within noise for the same steps, which matches what the torchao float8 docs report for Llama pretraining.
10:30 MEASURE — Val loss table: bf16, PTQ int4, QAT int4, FP8-trained. Loss curves for bf16 vs FP8. Tokens/s for bf16 vs FP8 training.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — QAT teaches the model to live on the grid; FP8 training puts the grid inside the matmul. Interview line: STE passes gradients straight through round, masked by the clamp range. With GPTQ, AWQ and FP8 in hand, project P8 is next: a W4A16 Triton kernel plugged into featherserve.
12:30 NEXT — Next: Prefill vs decode
key_math: x_hat = clamp(round(s x), -q_max, q_max)/s; STE: dL/dx = dL/dx_hat * 1[|s x| <= q_max]; x_hat = x + (fq(x) - x).detach(); FP8: s = 448 / amax (current or delayed)
code_task: fake_quant_ste(x, bits, group_size) -> x_hat same shape; QATLinear(in, out) replacing nn.Linear; train loop with three arms (PTQ, QAT, FP8 via torchao float8 conversion); val loss and throughput table.
receipt: assert torch.equal(grad, ((s*x).abs() <= q_max).float()) for the STE; val_loss(QAT int4) < val_loss(PTQ int4) after real quantization; FP8 training loss within noise of bf16 at the same step count.
gotchas: Using torch.round in forward without the detach trick gives zero gradients and the model silently stops learning; clamping without masking the gradient lets weights drift outside the range forever; FP8 training on small matrices is often slower than bf16 because of casting overhead, the speedup appears at larger hidden sizes.
interview_q: What is the straight-through estimator and why does QAT need it? Model answer: round has zero gradient almost everywhere, so QAT uses the identity as its backward pass inside the clamp range; this lets the weights adapt to quantization noise during training.
explainer: We plot round as a staircase. Its slope is flat everywhere except at the jumps, where it is infinite.
Backprop through that staircase gives zero gradient, so a model trained through it never moves.
The straight-through estimator draws a straight line over the staircase and uses its slope of one for backward.
Outside the clamp range the line goes flat, so weights that saturate stop receiving gradient.
During QAT, weights cluster near grid points. The rounding error histogram narrows step by step.
FP8 training is different. The matmul itself runs in FP8, with a scale chosen from each tensor's current maximum.
Final chart: bf16 and FP8 loss curves on top of each other, and QAT beating PTQ after conversion.

short: The staircase vs straight line STE beat. Caption: 'How you backprop through round().'
yt_title: Quantization-Aware Training and FP8 Training from Scratch
x_post: round() has zero gradient almost everywhere. QAT fixes it with one line: x_hat = x + (fq(x) - x).detach(). QAT int4 beat PTQ int4 on my small GPT, and FP8 training tracked the bf16 loss curve. Code + video:
linkedin: Today I closed out my quantization module with QAT and FP8 training. The straight-through estimator is one detach() line, and QAT int4 beat post-training int4 on my TinyStories GPT. FP8 training with torchao matched the bf16 loss curve. Next up: my own W4A16 Triton kernel for my inference engine.
